02 Assignment Part 1 · Select

The visualization under review

Evelina Gabasova’s Episode IV network is a rich public example: technically ambitious, immediately recognizable, and complex enough to support a meaningful redesign rather than a cosmetic restyle.

Original work

The Star Wars social network

Creator
Evelina Gabasova
Published
December 2015
Form
Force-directed weighted network
Data
Episode IV revised screenplay
Open the original article ↗ Open the archived dataset ↗
DATA

What the original data represents

Nodes are screenplay characters. A link is created when two characters speak within the same screenplay scene; its weight counts those shared speaking scenes. Node size represents the number of scenes attributed to a character. The published “all characters” version supplements R2-D2 and Chewbacca with mention-based approximations, an important methodological caveat for interpretation.

03 Assignment Part 2 · Analyze

Message, audience, and intended tasks

The graphic is best understood as an exploratory map of narrative relationships—not as chronology, emotional closeness, or literal screen time.

01 / Message

Reveal the social structure of the story

The visualization communicates which characters are prominent and connected, which pairs interact frequently, and how the cast separates into narrative groups. Viewers should notice Luke’s central position, the dense hero group, Imperial and Rebel-pilot clusters, and peripheral characters with few or weak connections.

02 / Audience

Fans first; visualization readers second

Its primary audience is general Star Wars fans curious about the film from a quantitative perspective. A secondary audience includes readers interested in data visualization, digital humanities, and introductory network analysis. Major character familiarity helps, but advanced statistics are not required.

03 / Tasks

Explore adjacency, prominence, and structure

  • Compare node sizes to identify prominent characters.
  • Determine whether two characters are connected.
  • Compare relationship frequency through link thickness.
  • Find central, peripheral, or bridging characters.
  • Recognize clusters and form an overview of network structure.
  • Hover for names and drag nodes to inspect crowded areas.

Operational definition: in the original, an “interaction” means two characters speak within the same screenplay scene. It does not measure sentiment or relationship quality.

04 Assignment Part 3 · Critique

What works—and what the hairball hides

The original succeeds as an overview, but its encoding and interaction design make precise comparison and methodological interpretation unnecessarily difficult.

2 Strengths

Intuitive relationship model

What works: nodes and links match the familiar mental model of a social network.

Why it matters: fans can quickly determine whether characters are connected without learning a specialized chart grammar.

Comprehensive, compact overview

What works: the view includes the broad Episode IV cast while using size and link width to encode two quantitative attributes.

Why it matters: it exposes major characters, minor groups, and network shape in one space-efficient display.

4 Opportunities

Ambiguous measures and preprocessing

Problem: the graphic itself does not clearly define a scene, interaction, node size, or the special handling of non-speaking characters.

Impact: viewers may misread co-speaking frequency as screen time or emotional closeness.

Response: surface definitions, legends, provenance, and limitations beside the redesigned views.

Edge crossings create a hairball

Problem: many nodes, labels, and overlapping links compete for attention.

Impact: tracing a pair or finding clusters becomes slow and error-prone.

Response: focus on eight principal characters and add selective highlighting.

Width is weak for exact comparison

Problem: unaligned edge widths are difficult to rank, and force-directed distance is not a quantitative scale.

Impact: viewers cannot reliably retrieve or compare relationship values.

Response: provide an adjacency matrix with aligned cells, ordered luminance, and exact counts.

Too little narrative context

Problem: the view shows aggregate connections but not where they occur or how individual prominence differs from connectivity.

Impact: it supports only a narrow set of exploratory tasks.

Response: add a composition view, scene-space map, and coordinated details on demand.

05 Assignment Part 4 · Redesign

Four views. One coordinated story.

The redesign intentionally focuses on eight principal characters rather than claiming they are the eight highest-ranked by a single noisy metric. Every view uses the same screenplay-derived presence definition and the same visual identity system.

480INT./EXT. screenplay scenes
300scenes containing a selected character
8principal characters, selected a priori

Unit: a revised-fourth-draft screenplay scene. Presence is detected from speaker cues and action text. These values are not finished-film screen time.

The focus set

Eight principal characters

Character colors remain stable across the network, matrix highlighting, treemap, and scene map. Color is never the only identifier: every character is also directly labeled.

Linked selection

All eight characters · select a node, cell, tile, or name to focus

View 01

A smaller, legible relationship network

Node area represents the number of screenplay scenes containing a character. Link width represents shared scenes. The fixed layout prevents continuous jitter; hover or select to isolate immediate relationships and retrieve exact values.

Node size = scenes Link width = shared scenes

View 02

An adjacency matrix for precise comparison

Every off-diagonal cell reports the number of screenplay scenes shared by a pair. Darker cells indicate larger values. Unlike unaligned link widths, the regular grid supports lookup, ranking, and cluster detection.

View 03

A treemap of character-scene appearances

Area shows each character’s share of all scene appearances accumulated by the eight selected characters. This additive denominator makes the treemap a valid part-to-whole display; it does not claim that character percentages partition movie runtime.

share = character scenes ÷ sum of all eight characters’ scenes

Narrative geography

Four operational spaces

Scene headings are coded into four mutually exclusive macro-locations. Ship interiors and general space scenes form “Outer Space / Spacecraft”; ambiguous cases follow the written heading and are disclosed as a limitation.

Tatooine

Desert, homestead, canyons, Mos Eisley, and Docking Bay 94.

Death Star

Station interiors, surface, gun emplacements, and trench scenes.

Yavin IV

Massassi temple, briefing room, war room, and Rebel hangars.

Outer Space / Spacecraft

Starships, hyperspace, fighter cockpits, and general space.

View 04

A radial scene-to-space map

The large outer orbit contains screenplay scenes in narrative order. Four smaller inner circles represent the operational spaces. Bundled paths connect each scene to its coded space; scene-dot size reports how many principal characters are present.

06 Assignment Part 5 · Explain

Design decisions and full report

Each intervention answers a specific critique. The goal is not more decoration—it is a broader and more reliable set of analytical tasks.

01

Filter with a declared rule

Changed: reduced the cast to eight principal characters.

Why: lower visual density makes topology traceable.

Addresses: crossings, occlusion, and unreadable labels.

Improves: adjacency and neighborhood identification.

02

Add an aligned comparison view

Changed: paired the network with a numbered matrix.

Why: aligned cells and luminance outperform floating widths for comparison.

Addresses: ambiguous ranking and value retrieval.

Improves: extrema, pair comparison, and cluster tasks.

03

Separate concepts of prominence

Changed: added a valid part-to-whole treemap.

Why: individual presence is not the same as connectivity.

Addresses: the original’s narrow information scope.

Improves: comparison of scene share against network position.

04

Restore narrative context

Changed: connected ordered scenes to four macro-locations.

Why: aggregate links hide where relationships occur.

Addresses: missing sequence and setting.

Improves: scene retrieval and spatial story tracing.

Submission report · 500–800 words

Visualization Critique and Redesign Report

Original visualization and context

Evelina Gabasova’s Episode IV: A New Hope social network is a force-directed node-link visualization derived from a revised screenplay. Characters form nodes; two characters are connected when they speak in the same scene. Node size represents the number of scenes attributed to a character, and link width represents shared speaking scenes. The intended message is that screenplay interactions reveal the film’s prominent characters, strongest recurring relationships, and narrative groups. The primary audience is Star Wars fans interested in a quantitative view of the film; secondary readers include visualization and digital-humanities audiences. Intended tasks include identifying prominent characters, determining adjacency, comparing relationship frequency, finding central or peripheral characters, and recognizing clusters.

Critique

The visualization has two important strengths. First, the node-link idiom is perceptually intuitive for relationship data: a viewer can quickly see whether two characters connect and form an overall impression of network structure. Second, it presents a broad cast compactly and uses node size and link width to encode quantitative attributes, making Luke and the densely connected principal group visually salient.

Its weaknesses limit more precise tasks. The graphic does not prominently define “interaction,” node value, scene segmentation, or the mention-based approximation used for R2-D2 and Chewbacca. This ambiguity can cause viewers to mistake shared speaking scenes for emotional closeness or screen time. The numerous labels and crossing edges also create the network “hairball” described in the course material; tracing one relationship becomes difficult. In addition, unaligned edge widths are harder to compare than position or aligned cells, while force-directed distance has no explicit quantitative meaning. Finally, the original provides little narrative context: it does not show where interactions occur, separate presence from connectivity, or support exact value retrieval beyond limited hover behavior.

Redesign rationale

The redesign makes four connected decisions. First, it focuses on eight principal characters selected before analysis and labels that scope explicitly. This sacrifices cast completeness but removes clutter and makes neighborhoods traceable. Second, a fixed node-link view preserves the original’s intuitive topology while an adjacency matrix supplies aligned cells, ordered luminance, exact counts, and sortable rows for comparison. Third, a treemap separates individual presence from relationship structure. Its area encodes each character’s share of the eight characters’ combined scene appearances—a genuine additive whole rather than the misleading percentage of movie runtime originally considered. Fourth, a radial map places relevant scenes in screenplay order and connects them to Tatooine, the Death Star, Yavin IV, or Outer Space/Spacecraft. Coordinated selection links all four views and provides details on demand without permanently adding clutter.

Original versus redesign

The redesign makes pairwise comparison, exact lookup, character focusing, and scene-location exploration substantially easier. It also distinguishes three ideas that the original compresses: network connectivity, individual scene presence, and narrative setting. Important limitations remain. The source is a January 1976 draft, so deleted material and rapid cross-cutting produce screenplay scenes that differ from the released film. Presence is inferred from speaker cues and action text rather than measured screen time, and four macro-locations simplify ambiguous ship and battle settings. Filtering also removes minor-character context, while treemap area remains less precise than a sorted bar. These trade-offs are documented so viewers can use the redesign for its intended comparative and exploratory tasks without overstating what the data measures.

Chapter 07 · Conclusion

The network was only the beginning.

By giving topology, comparison, composition, and narrative space their own coordinated views, the redesign turns an impressive overview into an explainable analytical system.

We hope you enjoy exploring a galaxy of data.
